# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. # Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (AB 1076) — notice requirement

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (b)(1) For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter, the employer shall, **by February 14, 2024, notify the employee** that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. (2) Notice shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee. (c) A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).

# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (SB 699)

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Any contract that is void under this chapter is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**. (b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. *Citation:* 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994)  
*Status in this library:* modified — see Sheshunoff (2006)

Held that a covenant not to compete must be ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement and set out a two-part test requiring that the consideration be given, and the covenant be designed to enforce the employee's return promise, **at the time the agreement is made**. **Status: the timing requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (2006); *Light* should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant.**

*Citation:* 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)  
*Status in this library:* in force

# Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court

*Citation:* 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992)  
*Status in this library:* in force

California follows Restatement §187: a contractual choice of law is enforced if the chosen state has a substantial relationship to the parties, unless the chosen law is contrary to a **fundamental policy** of California and California has a **materially greater interest** in the determination of the issue.
=========== restatement_187.md ===========
# Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.

# Ryan LLC v. Federal Trade Commission

*Citation:* 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The court held the FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority under §6(g) of the FTC Act to promulgate the Non-Compete Rule and that the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; it set the Rule aside with nationwide effect under the APA. The FTC's appeal to the Fifth Circuit was voluntarily dismissed in September 2025.

# Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson

*Citation:* 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The Texas Supreme Court held that a covenant not to compete in an at-will employment agreement is enforceable when the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting — **modifying *Light v. Centel Cellular* (1994)** to the extent *Light* required the consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made. The court emphasized that the core inquiry is the reasonableness of the restraint under §15.50.
=========== tex_bcc_15_50.md ===========
# Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.

# Personal jurisdiction over the employee in Texas

*Citation:* Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A forum-selection clause consenting to Travis County generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts. Two short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice; an injunction entered in Texas would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete.

# MEMORANDUM — PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

**To:** General Counsel, Meridian Robotics, Inc.
**From:** Outside counsel
**Date:** October 25, 2026
**Re:** Enforceability of §8 (24-month nationwide non-compete) against Wei-Lin Zhao; whether to file in Travis County, Texas

---

## 1. Question Presented

May Meridian Robotics realistically enforce §8 of Wei-Lin Zhao's employment agreement — a 24-month, nationwide covenant not to work for any business "engaged in the design or sale of autonomous mobile robots for warehouse logistics" — by filing suit in Travis County, Texas, under the agreement's Texas choice-of-law and Travis County forum clauses, where Zhao primarily resided and worked in California for the entire 940-day term, signed the standard engineer form without counsel, and starts at Kestrel Autonomy (Fremont, CA) on October 13, 2026?

Sub-questions: (a) which state's law governs §8's enforceability in each possible forum; (b) is §8 enforceable under Texas law and under California law; (c) can Zhao void the choice-of-law and forum clauses under Cal. Lab. Code §925; (d) what is Meridian's exposure under Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 for *filing*; (e) what is the effect of the missed §16600.1 (AB 1076) notice deadline; (f) what remedies and fee exposure does Meridian face?

## 2. Brief Answer

**Recommendation: do not file in Travis County, and do not send any §8 demand letter. Do not enforce §8 against Zhao.**

Probability ranges (our judgment on this record; each is decomposed in §4):

| Outcome | Probability |
|---|---|
| A Travis County court applies **Texas** substantive law to §8's enforceability | **15–25%** |
| Meridian obtains and keeps an injunction that actually stops Zhao working at Kestrel | **5–15%** |
| §8 is held void/unenforceable as written (void in CA; reformed at best in TX) | **75–90%** |
| If Meridian files or sends a §8 demand letter, Zhao obtains a fee award and/or a §16600.5 civil-violation finding against Meridian | **60–75%** |
| Meridian is the net payer (its own fees plus Zhao's fee award) on a filed case | **65–85%** |

The plain news: **Meridian's choice-of-law clause does not deliver Texas law — not even in the forum it selects.** The Texas Supreme Court's own conflicts rule (*DeSantis*, applying Restatement §187) refuses to honor a non-compete choice-of-law clause where the employee worked in the other state and that state has a materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy. Zhao's facts are the mirror image of *DeSantis*, and California's policy is expressly "fundamental" (*Application Group*) and now statutory and extraterritorial (§§16600(b)(1), 16600.5(a)–(b)). Independently, §925 lets Zhao void both clauses (he had no counsel), which puts the case in California and strips Travis County of consent-based jurisdiction.

Second piece of plain news: **filing is itself the liability.** Under §16600.5(b)–(d), *attempting* to enforce a void non-compete "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" is a civil violation, and a prevailing employee recovers injunctive relief, actual damages, **and** mandatory attorney's fees and costs (§16600.5(e)). Meridian also *entered into* a void clause on March 4, 2024 — 63 days after §16600.5 took effect — which is a violation under §16600.5(c) and §16600.1(a) with no enforcement required. Third: the AB 1076 notice project was "deprioritized" (ticket LO-233) and the statutory deadline (February 14, 2024) lapsed; that is a company-wide unfair-competition exposure (§16600.1(c)) that a lawsuit would surface and that the "deprioritized" ticket makes look willful.

Expected-value arithmetic on filing (inputs are labeled assumptions, §6): filing costs roughly **$309,000–$480,000** in expected spend, so an injunction would have to be worth **≈$3.1 million** to Meridian to break even at a 10% win probability. The injunction's realistic value on this record is near zero, because a Texas injunction would not be recognized in California where Zhao lives and works.

## 3. Facts (from `documents/`)

- **Offer:** Feb. 28, 2024, emailed by Austin HR to a candidate in Oakland, CA; states "fully remote from California."
- **Agreement:** sent 9:12 a.m. March 4, 2024; signed by DocuSign at 11:05 a.m. the same day — a **113-minute** decision window. No negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered; "standard form for all engineers."
- **Work location (contract itself):** "Remote — Employee's residence (Oakland, California)."
- **Term:** March 4, 2024 → Sept. 30, 2026 = **940 days (≈2.57 years; ≈30.9 months)**, all performed from Oakland, with **two** short trips to Austin HQ (onboarding week, March 2024; offsite, Oct. 2025).
- **§8:** 24 months post-termination, anywhere in the United States, no employment with or services to any business "engaged in the design or sale of autonomous mobile robots for warehouse logistics." Duration is **24 months against a 30.9-month tenure** — the restraint is ~78% as long as the employment itself and geographic scope is 100% of the U.S. §9: 12-month employee/customer non-solicit. §10: standard confidentiality/inventions. §14: Texas law; exclusive jurisdiction and venue in Travis County. §15: recital that Employee "acknowledg[ed] having had the opportunity to consult counsel" — contradicted by the HR file note ("no counsel involved").
- **Statutory backdrop dates:** SB 699 (§16600(b)(1), §16600.5) and AB 1076 (§16600.1) took effect **Jan. 1, 2024**; Zhao's contract was made **March 4, 2024 — 63 days later**. The AB 1076 notice deadline was **Feb. 14, 2024 — 19 days before Zhao was even hired**. The company-wide notice project was deprioritized and **no notice was sent to California employees**.
- **Departure:** resignation emailed Sept. 16, 2026, effective Sept. 30, 2026; new employer Kestrel Autonomy, Fremont, CA, warehouse AMRs; start **Oct. 13, 2026 — 13 days after separation**. Restraint window would otherwise run to **Sept. 30, 2028** (718 days remaining at his Kestrel start). Zhao states he took nothing and will honor confidentiality.
- **GC's question** was asked Oct. 2, 2026 — 11 days *before* the Kestrel start date.
- **Assumptions (flagged; see `QUESTIONS.md`):** Meridian is headquartered/incorporated in Texas (Austin HQ is in the file; state of incorporation is not); Zhao was at-will; Meridian did in fact disclose confidential information to Zhao in performance (§10 exists and he was a perception engineer), which matters to Texas ancillarity; Meridian has no evidence Zhao took anything; Meridian has not yet sent any demand letter; §8 appears in the standard form used for all engineers, including other California-resident engineers.

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Which law applies, and why — the clause does not control in either forum

Both possible forums use the same analytical frame, and both point to California.

**In Travis County (Meridian's chosen forum), Texas conflicts law governs.** Texas follows Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187 (*DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)). Under §187(2), the parties' chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction, or (b) the chosen law "would be contrary to a fundamental policy of a state which has a **materially greater interest** … and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice." Meridian clears (a) — a Texas employer with an Austin HQ has a substantial relationship with Texas, so that path is closed. Everything turns on (b), and *DeSantis* is directly on point: the Texas Supreme Court **refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause to a non-compete** because the state where the employee worked had the materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy on non-competes. Per the library, *DeSantis* "stands for the proposition that a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy."

Here the §188-style contacts all sit in California except the employer's location: contract formed with an Oakland candidate by email; signed in California by DocuSign; the contract itself fixes the work location as Oakland; 940 of 940 days of performance in California; Zhao domiciled in California; the alleged breach (working for a California competitor) in California; only two brief Austin visits. (Note: the library contains §187 but **not** the text of §188; the contact list above is our argument from the file, not a verified quotation.) On the "fundamental policy" element, *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.*, 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998), states California's policy against non-competes is "fundamental," and it applied §16600 over a **Maryland** employer's contrary choice-of-law clause for an employee recruited to work in California. Meridian's posture is weaker than Maryland's in *Application Group*, because Meridian's own contract designates California as the workplace.

Realistic assessment: a Travis County judge applying *DeSantis* in good faith should apply **California law to §8's enforceability**. We put the chance that Texas substantive law reaches §8 at **15–25%**, because conflicts rulings are forum-dependent and Meridian does have the two Austin trips, Austin payroll, and a §15 counsel recital to point at.

**In a California forum, the result is the same and firmer.** California follows §187 through *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992) — enforce the clause unless the chosen law is contrary to a fundamental California policy and California has a materially greater interest. *Application Group* applies that exception on facts materially like ours. §16600.5(a)–(b) then removes the "but he signed it in Texas under Texas law" argument by statute: a void contract is unenforceable "regardless of where and when … signed," and an employer "shall not attempt to enforce" it "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California."

**What the FTC Rule does not do.** The FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule (16 C.F.R. pt. 910) is **vacated** — set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024), with the FTC's appeal voluntarily dismissed in September 2025; the Rule never took effect. It provides no support in either direction and must not be cited in any filing.

### 4.2 Enforceability under Texas law (§§15.50–15.52) — at best a reformed covenant, no damages

If Texas law did apply, §8 still fares badly:

- **Ancillarity (§15.50(a)):** the covenant must be "ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made." *Light v. Centel Cellular* (Tex. 1994) is **modified** by *Sheshunoff Management Services v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006): an at-will agreement supports a covenant where the employer's return promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting, and *Light* "should not be cited" for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant. *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011), rejected a narrow "give rise" requirement and held consideration reasonably related to the employer's interest in goodwill can support a covenant. So Meridian probably clears ancillarity **if** it in fact disclosed confidential information to Zhao (assumed; see `QUESTIONS.md`). Do not brief the *Light* two-part timing test — it is no longer good law.
- **Reasonableness (§15.50(a)):** limits on time, geography and scope must be reasonable and impose no "greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee." Meridian bears that burden under **§15.51(b)** because the agreement's primary purpose is to obligate personal services. A **nationwide** ban on working for *any* business in the warehouse-AMR field, for **24 months**, in **any** role, imposed on a non-negotiating senior engineer as a condition of hire, is on its face far broader than a goodwill interest in the accounts and technology Zhao actually touched — the restraint outlasts three-quarters of his tenure and covers territory he never worked.
- **The Texas remedy is reformation, not damages (§15.51(c)):** if the limitations are unreasonable the court **shall** reform them and enforce the covenant as reformed, and **may not award damages for breach before reformation**. §15.52 makes §§15.51's procedures and remedies **exclusive**, preempting other enforceability criteria. So the best realistic Texas outcome is an order reforming §8 to something narrower (e.g., a shorter period keyed to Zhao's actual accounts/technology), enforced prospectively — not money for having hired at Kestrel, and not a nationwide ban.
- **Even that is unenforceable where it matters.** Per our jurisdiction note (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)): an injunction entered in Texas "would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete." Zhao lives, works and is employed in California. A reformed Texas covenant therefore has little operational value.

### 4.3 Enforceability under California law (§16600, *Edwards*) — void

Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600(a) voids "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind." As amended by SB 699, §16600(b)(1) directs that it be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context … **no matter how narrowly tailored**, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter," and (b)(2) declares that this is not a change in existing law. *Edwards* holds non-competes "are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions," and it **rejected the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" exception**, expressly disapproving *Campbell v. Board of Trustees* (9th Cir. 1987) and *General Commercial Packaging* (9th Cir. 1997). Both of those cases are marked **superseded** in the library; the narrow-restraint argument Meridian would want is not California law and must not be briefed. *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), forecloses the other tempting argument: the rule of reason applies to restraints in **business-to-business** contracts, and the Court distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void.

There is no statutory exception in play on these facts (Zhao is an employee, not a seller of a business or goodwill). §8 is **void** under California law. Note that the library's §16600 excerpt does not print the chapter's exception list, so we flag that as a research gap rather than assert that no exception could ever apply.

As to §9 (12-month non-solicit, running to Sept. 30, 2027): §16600's text and its "read broadly" command make it likely void in California too, but **the library contains no authority applying §16600 to a non-solicitation clause**, so we label that conclusion unverified. Treat §9 as unenforceable against Zhao for practical purposes and do not threaten it (see §4.5 — an "attempt to enforce" a void provision is the violation).

### 4.4 Cal. Lab. Code §925 — Zhao can void both clauses

§925(a) bars an employer from requiring an employee **who primarily resides and works in California**, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that (1) requires adjudication outside California of a claim arising in California, or (2) deprives the employee of the substantive protection of California law for a controversy arising in California. §14 does both. Under §925(b) such a provision is **voidable by the employee**, and if voided at his request, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and **California law shall govern** the dispute." §925(c) permits the court to award the employee reasonable attorney's fees.

Elements on this record: Zhao primarily resided and worked in California (contract says so); the clause was imposed as a condition of employment (standard form for all engineers, signed 113 minutes after receipt, "no negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered"); and the contract post-dates §925(f)'s January 1, 2017 coverage date (entered March 4, 2024).

**The §925(e) escape hatch does not help Meridian.** §925(e) excludes only a contract with an employee who "**in fact** [is] **individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating** the terms" of the forum or choice-of-law provisions. Zhao was not represented at all. The §15 recital ("opportunity to consult counsel") is boilerplate contradicted by Meridian's own HR file note ("no counsel involved") — on these facts it is at most a fact dispute that the HR timeline resolves against us, and an "opportunity" is not "in fact … represented … in negotiating."

Two genuine soft spots, stated plainly: (i) §925(a) is keyed to a "claim arising in California" / "controversy arising in California," and Meridian can argue its claim arises from a Texas-law contract made by a Texas employer — though the employment, the breach and the harm all sit in California; (ii) the library's §925 text speaks of an "employee," and whether Zhao may invoke §925 **after** separation (he resigned Sept. 30, 2026) is not addressed by the material in the library — we flag that as unverified. Even if §925 failed, the §4.1 conflicts analysis reaches the same destination in a California forum.

**Jurisdictional consequence.** Our jurisdiction note: the forum clause "generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction," **but** "if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts," and "[t]wo short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice" under §17.042 and *Michiana*. So if Zhao makes his §925 election, Meridian may not even be able to hang a Texas judgment on him personally — the *Michiana* contract-plus-two-visits pattern is a coin flip, not a comfortable win.

### 4.5 §16600.5 exposure — the act of suing is the violation

§16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024) provides: (a) a contract void under the chapter "is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**"; (b) an employer "shall not **attempt to enforce**" such a contract "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California"; (c) an employer "shall not **enter into** a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter"; (d) an employer that enters into or attempts to enforce such a contract "commits a **civil violation**"; (e)(1) the employee or former employee may sue for injunctive relief or actual damages, or both; (e)(2) a prevailing employee or former employee "shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs."

Applied here:
1. **Entry violation (already occurred, no suit required).** On March 4, 2024 — 63 days after §16600.5 took effect — Meridian entered into a contract containing a clause void under §16600, as to Zhao and, per the file, as to every engineer on the standard form who resides/works in California. That is a §16600.5(c)–(d) civil violation and a §16600.1(a) unlawful inclusion sitting in Meridian's own form.
2. **Enforcement attempt (triggered by Meridian's own conduct).** Filing in Travis County is the paradigm "attempt to enforce." Whether a **pre-suit demand or reservation-of-rights letter** citing §8 also qualifies is not resolved by the library text, but "attempt to enforce" is broad enough that we would not send one; a letter is a low-cost way for Meridian to convert a passive exposure into an active claim. Zhao has already retained California counsel who is telling him §8 is void and that he may void the forum and choice-of-law clauses — he is positioned to plead §16600.5 cross-claims the day Meridian files.
3. **Fee-shifting is one-way and partly mandatory.** §16600.5(e)(2) fees to a prevailing former employee, plus §925(c) discretionary fees, plus Zhao's actual damages. There is no mirror-image fee provision for Meridian anywhere in the library.

### 4.6 AB 1076 / §16600.1 notice issue — a self-inflicted, company-wide exposure

§16600.1(a) makes it "unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement," that does not satisfy a chapter exception. §16600.1(b)(1) required the employer, **by February 14, 2024**, to notify current employees and former employees employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include such a clause, that it is **void**; (b)(2) prescribes the form — an individualized written communication delivered to **both** the last known mailing address and the email address. §16600.1(c): a violation "constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)."

Facts: "no notice was sent to California employees"; the project was "deprioritized" per legal-ops ticket **LO-233**, dated 2024-02-14 — the statutory deadline itself. That ticket is discoverable, contemporaneous, and reads as a knowing decision not to comply.

Three consequences:
- **Zhao individually.** The notice deadline (Feb. 14, 2024) expired **19 days before Zhao was hired** (Mar. 4, 2024). The library's text does not say what the notice duty means for an employee hired after the deadline passed, so there is a real argument that §16600.1(b) imposed no notice obligation as to Zhao (the deadline was fixed and past). We flag this as genuinely unsettled on the library. It is a small point of comfort only: his exposure runs through §16600.1(a) (unlawful inclusion) and §16600.5(c) (unlawful entry), neither of which depends on notice.
- **The rest of the population.** Every California current employee, and every California former employee employed after Jan. 1, 2022, who signed the §8 form was entitled to notice by Feb. 14, 2024 and got none. That is a §17200 unfair-competition theory, and its size scales with the affected headcount — which we do not have (see `QUESTIONS.md`). A Meridian-initiated lawsuit against Zhao is the single most reliable way to advertise that theory to the population that could assert it.
- **Remedial limits of our advice.** The library does **not** contain §17200 itself, so we cannot verify §17200's remedies, limitations period, or class mechanics from this library; we flag that rather than assert a restitution number.

Also relevant to Meridian's framing: our own prior work product is a liability. `memo_bank/firm_memo_2024_remote_employees.md` recommended suing in Travis County in the *Alvarez* matter on the strength of *Calderon v. Pacific Dynamics Corp.* and *Westbrook Systems, Inc. v. Ng* — **neither of which is in this library**, so neither can be verified or cited in a filing here. `memo_bank/firm_memo_2025_update.md` reports the Ninth Circuit granted rehearing **en banc** in *Westbrook* (argued Jan. 2025), so even the persuasive backbone of that advice was under review. The 2024 memo's theory also collides with *DeSantis* and *Application Group*, both in force in this library. Expect plaintiff's counsel to obtain the 2024 memo in discovery if Meridian files; "outside counsel told us to sue" is not a defense and may undercut any good-faith narrative on the §16600.1/§16600.5 claims.

### 4.7 Remedies and fee exposure

**Meridian's upside, best realistic case:** Texas law applied (15–25%) → §8 reformed under §15.51(c) → prospective injunction on narrowed terms; **no damages for pre-reformation breach** (§15.51(c)); enforcement of that injunction in California meets non-recognition. A California forum forecloses even this.

**Meridian's downside:** Zhao's injunctive relief and actual damages under §16600.5(e)(1) (his lost opportunity, moving costs, counseling costs — facts we do not have); **mandatory** fees and costs under §16600.5(e)(2); §925(c) fees; §16600.1(c)/§17200 exposure across the California population; Meridian's own fees; plus reputational and recruiting damage from publicly suing a rank-and-file engineer who signed a form in two hours and is joining a Fremont competitor.

**Arithmetic (illustrative inputs, explicitly assumed — not client-supplied):**
- Zhao's fee exposure if we file: 120–300 hours × $550–$850 blended = **$66,000–$255,000**.
- Expected cost of filing to Meridian, at P(lose) = 0.90 and an assumed Meridian spend of $250,000: $250,000 + 0.90 × $66,000 = **$309,400**; $250,000 + 0.90 × $255,000 = **$479,500**.
- Break-even value of an injunction at P(win) = 0.10: 0.10 × V = $309,400 → **V ≈ $3,094,000**. Nothing in this file supports an injunction worth ~$3.1M; the covenant's only measurable asset is 24 months of exclusion covering a field in which Meridian competes nationally, and Zhao's own role in it is limited to what he actually touched.
- Notice-population exposure is not quantifiable on this record: it scales with the number of California current/former engineers on the §8 form (headcount requested in `QUESTIONS.md`).

These figures do not reconcile to anything in the file and we do not force them to: the headcount, Zhao's actual damages, and §17200 remedies are all unknown.

## 5. Strongest argument for each side

**Meridian's best argument.** Texas has a substantial relationship to this contract (Texas employer, Austin HQ, Austin payroll, Travis County venue, §15 counsel recital), so §187(2)(a) is satisfied and the clause should be honored. *DeSantis* is distinguishable because there the Texas Supreme Court protected **Texas's** interest in an employee **working in Texas**; nothing in *DeSantis* obliges a Texas court to subordinate Texas's own legitimate interest in protecting Texas-owned goodwill to the policy of a state the employee never left, and Zhao did voluntarily accept a Texas forum and made two Austin trips. Then, under §§15.50–15.52, §8 does not die: it is ancillary (Zhao received confidential information; *Sheshunoff*, *Marsh*), and any overbreadth in its 24-month/nationwide limits is cured by **mandatory reformation** under §15.51(c) — with §15.52's exclusivity preempting extra-statutory defenses. A Texas judgment on a reformed covenant entered by a court with consent-based jurisdiction (jurisdiction note) is valid where entered, and *Advanced Bionics* means California courts generally will not enjoin Meridian from litigating in Texas.

**Zhao's best argument.** §8 is void under §16600 as amended, and *Edwards* kills any narrow-tailoring defense — §16600(b)(1) now says "no matter how narrowly tailored," and *Ixchel* confines the rule of reason to business-to-business deals. §16600.5(a)–(b) makes the place of signing and the Texas forum irrelevant, and makes Meridian's *filing itself* a civil violation carrying mandatory fees. §925 lets Zhao void both clauses (no counsel, form contract, California residence and work, post-2017 contract), which sends the case to California under California law and removes consent-based jurisdiction in Travis County, where *Michiana* contacts are doubtful in any event. And even if Meridian wins everywhere in Texas, the jurisdiction note concedes the injunction "would face non-recognition in California" — so Meridian can win a judgment it cannot collect in behavior terms, while paying both sides' fees. Add the §16600.1(c) notice failure, and Meridian's suit is a $300k–$480k expected-cost advertisement for the strongest claim against it.

## 6. Recommendation

1. **Do not file in Travis County. Do not sue Zhao.** There is no realistic path to an injunction that changes behavior, and §16600.5(b)–(e) makes the filing the trigger for liability and mandatory fees.
2. **Send no §8 demand, reservation-of-rights, or "we note your obligations under §8" letter.** Attempted enforcement is the violation. If a communication is unavoidable, limit it to (a) acknowledging his separation, (b) confirming that §10 confidentiality/invention obligations continue, and (c) making no reference to §8 or §9 and no request that he not work at Kestrel — cleared by California counsel before it goes out. Note: we cannot verify from this library whether California treats a broad NDA as a void restraint; get that checked.

## 3. Facts (from `documents/`)

- **Offer:** Feb. 28, 2024, emailed by Austin HR to a candidate in Oakland, CA; states "fully remote from California."

The AB 1076 notice deadline was **Feb. 14, 2024 — 19 days before Zhao was even hired**. The company-wide notice project was deprioritized and **no notice was sent to California employees**.

Restraint window would otherwise run to **Sept. 30, 2028** (718 days remaining at his Kestrel start). Zhao states he took nothing and will honor confidentiality.
- **GC's question** was asked Oct. 2, 2026 — 11 days *before* the Kestrel start date.

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Which law applies, and why — the clause does not control in either forum

Both possible forums use the same analytical frame, and both point to California.

**In Travis County (Meridian's chosen forum), Texas conflicts law governs.** Texas follows Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187 (*DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)). Under §187(2), the parties' chosen law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction, or (b) the chosen law "would be contrary to a fundamental policy of a state which has a **materially greater interest** … and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice." Meridian clears (a) — a Texas employer with an Austin HQ has a substantial relationship with Texas, so that path is closed. Everything turns on (b), and *DeSantis* is directly on point: the Texas Supreme Court **refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause to a non-compete** because the state where the employee worked had the materially greater interest and a fundamental contrary policy on non-competes. Per the library, *DeSantis* "stands for the proposition that a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy."

Here the §188-style contacts all sit in California except the employer's location: contract formed with an Oakland candidate by email; signed in California by DocuSign; the contract itself fixes the work location as Oakland; 940 of 940 days of performance in California; Zhao domiciled in California; the alleged breach (working for a California competitor) in California; only two brief Austin visits. (Note: the library contains §187 but **not** the text of §188; the contact list above is our argument from the file, not a verified quotation.) On the "fundamental policy" element, *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.*, 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998), states California's policy against non-competes is "fundamental," and it applied §16600 over a **Maryland** employer's contrary choice-of-law clause for an employee recruited to work in California. Meridian's posture is weaker than Maryland's in *Application Group*, because Meridian's own contract designates California as the workplace.

Realistic assessment: a Travis County judge applying *DeSantis* in good faith should apply **California law to §8's enforceability**. We put the chance that Texas substantive law reaches §8 at **15–25%**, because conflicts rulings are forum-dependent and Meridian does have the two Austin trips, Austin payroll, and a §15 counsel recital to point at.

**In a California forum, the result is the same and firmer.** California follows §187 through *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992) — enforce the clause unless the chosen law is contrary to a fundamental California policy and California has a materially greater interest. *Application Group* applies that exception on facts materially like ours. §16600.5(a)–(b) then removes the "but he signed it in Texas under Texas law" argument by statute: a void contract is unenforceable "regardless of where and when … signed," and an employer "shall not attempt to enforce" it "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California."

**What the FTC Rule does not do.** The FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule (16 C.F.R. pt. 910) is **vacated** — set aside nationwide in *Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024), with the FTC's appeal voluntarily dismissed in September 2025; the Rule never took effect. It provides no support in either direction and must not be cited in any filing.

### 4.2 Enforceability under Texas law (§§15.50–15.52) — at best a reformed covenant, no damages

If Texas law did apply, §8 still fares badly:

- **Ancillarity (§15.50(a)):** the covenant must be "ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made." *Light v. Centel Cellular* (Tex. 1994) is **modified** by *Sheshunoff Management Services v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006): an at-will agreement supports a covenant where the employer's return promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting, and *Light* "should not be cited" for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant. *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011), rejected a narrow "give rise" requirement and held consideration reasonably related to the employer's interest in goodwill can support a covenant. So Meridian probably clears ancillarity **if** it in fact disclosed confidential information to Zhao (assumed; see `QUESTIONS.md`). Do not brief the *Light* two-part timing test — it is no longer good law.
- **Reasonableness (§15.50(a)):** limits on time, geography and scope must be reasonable and impose no "greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee." Meridian bears that burden under **§15.51(b)** because the agreement's primary purpose is to obligate personal services. A **nationwide** ban on working for *any* business in the warehouse-AMR field, for **24 months**, in **any** role, imposed on a non-negotiating senior engineer as a condition of hire, is on its face far broader than a goodwill interest in the accounts and technology Zhao actually touched — the restraint outlasts three-quarters of his tenure and covers territory he never worked.
- **The Texas remedy is reformation, not damages (§15.51(c)):** if the limitations are unreasonable the court **shall** reform them and enforce the covenant as reformed, and **may not award damages for breach before reformation**. §15.52 makes §§15.51's procedures and remedies **exclusive**, preempting other enforceability criteria. So the best realistic Texas outcome is an order reforming §8 to something narrower (e.g., a shorter period keyed to Zhao's actual accounts/technology), enforced prospectively — not money for having hired at Kestrel, and not a nationwide ban.
- **Even that is unenforceable where it matters.** Per our jurisdiction note (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)): an injunction entered in Texas "would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete." Zhao lives, works and is employed in California. A reformed Texas covenant therefore has little operational value.

### 4.3 Enforceability under California law (§16600, *Edwards*) — void

Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600(a) voids "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind." As amended by SB 699, §16600(b)(1) directs that it be "read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context … **no matter how narrowly tailored**, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter," and (b)(2) declares that this is not a change in existing law. *Edwards* holds non-competes "are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions," and it **rejected the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" exception**, expressly disapproving *Campbell v. Board of Trustees* (9th Cir. 1987) and *General Commercial Packaging* (9th Cir. 1997). Both of those cases are marked **superseded** in the library; the narrow-restraint argument Meridian would want is not California law and must not be briefed. *Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), forecloses the other tempting argument: the rule of reason applies to restraints in **business-to-business** contracts, and the Court distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void.

There is no statutory exception in play on these facts (Zhao is an employee, not a seller of a business or goodwill). §8 is **void** under California law. Note that the library's §16600 excerpt does not print the chapter's exception list, so we flag that as a research gap rather than assert that no exception could ever apply.

As to §9 (12-month non-solicit, running to Sept. 30, 2027): §16600's text and its "read broadly" command make it likely void in California too, but **the library contains no authority applying §16600 to a non-solicitation clause**, so we label that conclusion unverified. Treat §9 as unenforceable against Zhao for practical purposes and do not threaten it (see §4.5 — an "attempt to enforce" a void provision is the violation).

### 4.4 Cal. Lab. Code §925 — Zhao can void both clauses

§925(a) bars an employer from requiring an employee **who primarily resides and works in California**, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that (1) requires adjudication outside California of a claim arising in California, or (2) deprives the employee of the substantive protection of California law for a controversy arising in California. §14 does both. Under §925(b) such a provision is **voidable by the employee**, and if voided at his request, "the matter shall be adjudicated in California and **California law shall govern** the dispute." §925(c) permits the court to award the employee reasonable attorney's fees.

Elements on this record: Zhao primarily resided and worked in California (contract says so); the clause was imposed as a condition of employment (standard form for all engineers, signed 113 minutes after receipt, "no negotiation; no attorney review requested or offered"); and the contract post-dates §925(f)'s January 1, 2017 coverage date (entered March 4, 2024).

**The §925(e) escape hatch does not help Meridian.** §925(e) excludes only a contract with an employee who "**in fact** [is] **individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating** the terms" of the forum or choice-of-law provisions. Zhao was not represented at all. The §15 recital ("opportunity to consult counsel") is boilerplate contradicted by Meridian's own HR file note ("no counsel involved") — on these facts it is at most a fact dispute that the HR timeline resolves against us, and an "opportunity" is not "in fact … represented … in negotiating."

Two genuine soft spots, stated plainly: (i) §925(a) is keyed to a "claim arising in California" / "controversy arising in California," and Meridian can argue its claim arises from a Texas-law contract made by a Texas employer — though the employment, the breach and the harm all sit in California; (ii) the library's §925 text speaks of an "employee," and whether Zhao may invoke §925 **after** separation (he resigned Sept. 30, 2026) is not addressed by the material in the library — we flag that as unverified. Even if §925 failed, the §4.1 conflicts analysis reaches the same destination in a California forum.

**Jurisdictional consequence.** Our jurisdiction note: the forum clause "generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction," **but** "if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts," and "[t]wo short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice" under §17.042 and *Michiana*. So if Zhao makes his §925 election, Meridian may not even be able to hang a Texas judgment on him personally — the *Michiana* contract-plus-two-visits pattern is a coin flip, not a comfortable win.

### 4.5 §16600.5 exposure — the act of suing is the violation

§16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024) provides: (a) a contract void under the chapter "is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**"; (b) an employer "shall not **attempt to enforce**" such a contract "regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California"; (c) an employer "shall not **enter into** a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter"; (d) an employer that enters into or attempts to enforce such a contract "commits a **civil violation**"; (e)(1) the employee or former employee may sue for injunctive relief or actual damages, or both; (e)(2) a prevailing employee or former employee "shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs."

Applied here:
1. **Entry violation (already occurred, no suit required).** On March 4, 2024 — 63 days after §16600.5 took effect — Meridian entered into a contract containing a clause void under §16600, as to Zhao and, per the file, as to every engineer on the standard form who resides/works in California. That is a §16600.5(c)–(d) civil violation and a §16600.1(a) unlawful inclusion sitting in Meridian's own form.
2. **Enforcement attempt (triggered by Meridian's own conduct).** Filing in Travis County is the paradigm "attempt to enforce." Whether a **pre-suit demand or reservation-of-rights letter** citing §8 also qualifies is not resolved by the library text, but "attempt to enforce" is broad enough that we would not send one; a letter is a low-cost way for Meridian to convert a passive exposure into an active claim. Zhao has already retained California counsel who is telling him §8 is void and that he may void the forum and choice-of-law clauses — he is positioned to plead §16600.5 cross-claims the day Meridian files.
3. **Fee-shifting is one-way and partly mandatory.** §16600.5(e)(2) fees to a prevailing former employee, plus §925(c) discretionary fees, plus Zhao's actual damages. There is no mirror-image fee provision for Meridian anywhere in the library.

### 4.6 AB 1076 / §16600.1 notice issue — a self-inflicted, company-wide exposure

§16600.1(a) makes it "unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement," that does not satisfy a chapter exception. §16600.1(b)(1) required the employer, **by February 14, 2024**, to notify current employees and former employees employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include such a clause, that it is **void**; (b)(2) prescribes the form — an individualized written communication delivered to **both** the last known mailing address and the email address. §16600.1(c): a violation "constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)."

Facts: "no notice was sent to California employees"; the project was "deprioritized" per legal-ops ticket **LO-233**, dated 2024-02-14 — the statutory deadline itself. That ticket is discoverable, contemporaneous, and reads as a knowing decision not to comply.

Three consequences:
- **Zhao individually.** The notice deadline (Feb. 14, 2024) expired **19 days before Zhao was hired** (Mar. 4, 2024). The library's text does not say what the notice duty means for an employee hired after the deadline passed, so there is a real argument that §16600.1(b) imposed no notice obligation as to Zhao (the deadline was fixed and past). We flag this as genuinely unsettled on the library. It is a small point of comfort only: his exposure runs through §16600.1(a) (unlawful inclusion) and §16600.5(c) (unlawful entry), neither of which depends on notice.
- **The rest of the population.** Every California current employee, and every California former employee employed after Jan. 1, 2022, who signed the §8 form was entitled to notice by Feb. 14, 2024 and got none. That is a §17200 unfair-competition theory, and its size scales with the affected headcount — which we do not have (see `QUESTIONS.md`). A Meridian-initiated lawsuit against Zhao is the single most reliable way to advertise that theory to the population that could assert it.
- **Remedial limits of our advice.** The library does **not** contain §17200 itself, so we cannot verify §17200's remedies, limitations period, or class mechanics from this library; we flag that rather than assert a restitution number.

Also relevant to Meridian's framing: our own prior work product is a liability. `memo_bank/firm_memo_2024_remote_employees.md` recommended suing in Travis County in the *Alvarez* matter on the strength of *Calderon v. Pacific Dynamics Corp.* and *Westbrook Systems, Inc. v. Ng* — **neither of which is in this library**, so neither can be verified or cited in a filing here. `memo_bank/firm_memo_2025_update.md` reports the Ninth Circuit granted rehearing **en banc** in *Westbrook* (argued Jan. 2025), so even the persuasive backbone of that advice was under review. The 2024 memo's theory also collides with *DeSantis* and *Application Group*, both in force in this library. Expect plaintiff's counsel to obtain the 2024 memo in discovery if Meridian files; "outside counsel told us to sue" is not a defense and may undercut any good-faith narrative on the §16600.1/§16600.5 claims.

### 4.7 Remedies and fee exposure

**Meridian's upside, best realistic case:** Texas law applied (15–25%) → §8 reformed under §15.51(c) → prospective injunction on narrowed terms; **no damages for pre-reformation breach** (§15.51(c)); enforcement of that injunction in California meets non-recognition. A California forum forecloses even this.

**Meridian's downside:** Zhao's injunctive relief and actual damages under §16600.5(e)(1) (his lost opportunity, moving costs, counseling costs — facts we do not have); **mandatory** fees and costs under §16600.5(e)(2); §925(c) fees; §16600.1(c)/§17200 exposure across the California population; Meridian's own fees; plus reputational and recruiting damage from publicly suing a rank-and-file engineer who signed a form in two hours and is joining a Fremont competitor.

**Arithmetic (illustrative inputs, explicitly assumed — not client-supplied):**
- Zhao's fee exposure if we file: 120–300 hours × $550–$850 blended = **$66,000–$255,000**.
- Expected cost of filing to Meridian, at P(lose) = 0.90 and an assumed Meridian spend of $250,000: $250,000 + 0.90 × $66,000 = **$309,400**; $250,000 + 0.90 × $255,000 = **$479,500**.
- Break-even value of an injunction at P(win) = 0.10: 0.10 × V = $309,400 → **V ≈ $3,094,000**. Nothing in this file supports an injunction worth ~$3.1M; the covenant's only measurable asset is 24 months of exclusion covering a field in which Meridian competes nationally, and Zhao's own role in it is limited to what he actually touched.
- Notice-population exposure is not quantifiable on this record: it scales with the number of California current/former engineers on the §8 form (headcount requested in `QUESTIONS.md`).

These figures do not reconcile to anything in the file and we do not force them to: the headcount, Zhao's actual damages, and §17200 remedies are all unknown.

## 5. Strongest argument for each side

**Meridian's best argument.** Texas has a substantial relationship to this contract (Texas employer, Austin HQ, Austin payroll, Travis County venue, §15 counsel recital), so §187(2)(a) is satisfied and the clause should be honored. *DeSantis* is distinguishable because there the Texas Supreme Court protected **Texas's** interest in an employee **working in Texas**; nothing in *DeSantis* obliges a Texas court to subordinate Texas's own legitimate interest in protecting Texas-owned goodwill to the policy of a state the employee never left, and Zhao did voluntarily accept a Texas forum and made two Austin trips. Then, under §§15.50–15.52, §8 does not die: it is ancillary (Zhao received confidential information; *Sheshunoff*, *Marsh*), and any overbreadth in its 24-month/nationwide limits is cured by **mandatory reformation** under §15.51(c) — with §15.52's exclusivity preempting extra-statutory defenses. A Texas judgment on a reformed covenant entered by a court with consent-based jurisdiction (jurisdiction note) is valid where entered, and *Advanced Bionics* means California courts generally will not enjoin Meridian from litigating in Texas.

**Zhao's best argument.** §8 is void under §16600 as amended, and *Edwards* kills any narrow-tailoring defense — §16600(b)(1) now says "no matter how narrowly tailored," and *Ixchel* confines the rule of reason to business-to-business deals. §16600.5(a)–(b) makes the place of signing and the Texas forum irrelevant, and makes Meridian's *filing itself* a civil violation carrying mandatory fees. §925 lets Zhao void both clauses (no counsel, form contract, California residence and work, post-2017 contract), which sends the case to California under California law and removes consent-based jurisdiction in Travis County, where *Michiana* contacts are doubtful in any event. And even if Meridian wins everywhere in Texas, the jurisdiction note concedes the injunction "would face non-recognition in California" — so Meridian can win a judgment it cannot collect in behavior terms, while paying both sides' fees. Add the §16600.1(c) notice failure, and Meridian's suit is a $300k–$480k expected-cost advertisement for the strongest claim against it.

## 6. Recommendation

1. **Do not file in Travis County. Do not sue Zhao.** There is no realistic path to an injunction that changes behavior, and §16600.5(b)–(e) makes the filing the trigger for liability and mandatory fees.
2. **Send no §8 demand, reservation-of-rights, or "we note your obligations under §8" letter.** Attempted enforcement is the violation. # Questions for the client (Meridian Robotics)

Answering these would let us tighten the probabilities and put real numbers on the exposure. The memo's core recommendation (**do not file; do not send a §8 demand; cure the AB 1076 notice gap**) does not depend on any of these answers.

**A. Facts bearing on the Texas-law fallback (the only branch where §8 could survive at all)**

1. Does the full agreement (beyond the excerpt) contain a Meridian promise to provide confidential information / specialized training, and did Meridian in fact deliver it to Zhao? We assumed yes (§10 exists; he was a perception engineer). Under *Sheshunoff* (209 S.W.3d 644) the promise must have been **performed**; if there was no reciprocal promise, §8 fails the §15.50(a) ancillarity test even under Texas law.
2. Is the agreement an at-will agreement, and was Zhao offered anything at signing beyond continued at-will employment (bonus, equity, training reimbursement)? Relevant to *Marsh USA v. Cook* goodwill consideration.
3. What did Zhao actually work on — which named accounts, roadmap programs, or pricing did he touch? This sets the ceiling on what goodwill §8 could arguably protect, i.e. how far a Texas court could reform §8 under §15.51(c).
4. Does Meridian have any **evidence** (access logs, downloads, device transfer) that Zhao took confidential material? The file contains none, and Zhao denies it. Without evidence there is no covenant-independent claim to bring.

**B. Facts bearing on Meridian's own exposure (please route through privilege)**

5. How many **current** employees and **former** employees (employed after Jan. 1, 2022) resident/worked in California signed an agreement containing the §8 clause or the §9 non-solicit? This is the size of the §16600.1(b)/§17200 population. Give us the number and the states, not the names.
6. Is the §8 clause (and the Texas law / Travis County clause) still in the current engineer form, and is it still being presented to California-resident hires? §16600.5(c) and §16600.1(a) make *entering into* such a contract unlawful, so a continuing practice is a continuing violation.
7. Has Meridian sent Zhao **any** communication referring to §8 or §9 (letter, email, call from HR, exit-interview script)? If something has already gone out, our §16600.5(b) exposure analysis changes and we need it immediately.
8. What is the status of legal-ops ticket **LO-233** — who deprioritized it, when, and are there related emails? A litigation hold is needed; that ticket is the most damaging document we have seen.
9. Zhao's actual damages as he would plead them (Kestrel compensation delta, relocation, any period of non-employment) — §16600.5(e)(1) allows actual damages, and we cannot size that number.
10. Meridian's own budgeted litigation spend for a Travis County non-compete case (we assumed $250,000) and whether the GC wants the California-employee notice cure costed out as a line item.

**C. Strategy questions**

11. Is Meridian's real objective (a) stopping Zhao specifically, (b) deterring other engineers from going to Kestrel, or (c) protecting specific technology/accounts? (b) is precisely the objective a §16600.5 lawsuit would defeat, and the notice cure will make the form unenforceable against everyone in California.
12. Are there *other* planned departures to California competitors this year, and does any involve an employee who **was** individually represented by counsel in negotiating forum/choice-of-law terms (§925(e) is the only safe harbor we have, and it is narrow)?
13. Do you want us to prepare (i) the §16600.1(b)(2)-compliant notice letters and (ii) a California-law form for California-resident hires, on a privileged basis?
